A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mode-test and weak-guidance research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original mode tests, guidance experiments, image-quality measurements and demographic-bias evaluations, including additional results in Appendices B and C.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments across Stable Diffusion versions, including new SD3 results, simultaneous gender/race debiasing and a 40-participant human evaluation.

M1.justification: For SD1.5/SDXL, v1 alternates original and modified text conditions throughout denoising; v2 introduces an initial modified-condition-only phase before alternation (Section 4.1). V2 also adapts guidance to SD3's encoders and combines separately sampled gender and race embeddings (Appendices A.3 and C.4). These extend the existing additive weak-guidance method.

E1.justification: V2 adds simultaneous gender and race debiasing (Appendix C.4), whereas v1 evaluates these separately. The eight-profession study, 35-profession/five-template test, binary gender categories, five racial categories and COCO caption-generation domain are retained.

E2.justification: V2's design comparison adds appending an attribute word to the prompt (Figure 7), replacing the explicit in-sentence attribute specification comparison in v1 Figure 8. The principal evaluated baselines—FairDiffusion, UCE, FTDiff and SelfDisc—remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes from FID and CLIP evaluation on COCO-2017-5k to CMMD and CLIP evaluation on COCO-2014-30k. V2 adds SD3 experiments using 28 FlowMatchEulerDiscrete steps, plus a 40-participant survey using image groups and comparative judgments. Appendix C.4 introduces a multiclass discrepancy metric for the additional evaluations.

E4.justification: V2 adds SD2/SDXL mode tests, SD3 guidance sensitivity analyses, separate-versus-simultaneous attribute guidance comparisons and human validation. It revises the main design ablation and removes v1 Appendix B.2–B.3's SD2/SDXL timing and design-choice analyses, including their CLIP-score comparisons.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations over three runs of 100 images for attribute-specified prompts and across five templates for prompt generalization. V2's main-text reference to 300 images is consistent with the retained three-by-100 protocol. No new confidence intervals, significance tests or seed-reporting practice is introduced.

E6.justification: Numerous retained results change, and SD3, joint-debiasing and human outcomes are added. The proposed method's CEO female ratio across prompt templates changes from 0.28±0.10 to 0.06±0.09 (v1 Table 6; v2 Table S7). FairDiffusion's SD2 fashion-designer ratio changes from 0.406 to 0.088 (Table 5; Table S6). COCO scores use different protocols and cannot establish same-setting gains. V2 Table 2 reports an average discrepancy of 0.167 although its eight proposed-method entries imply approximately 0.163.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix C.4, Equation 2 introduces a formal multiclass discrepancy definition using deviations from uniform attribute probabilities, extending v1's binary balance reporting. The existing CADS and attribute-embedding equations are retained; neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: V1 claims intrinsic fairness in SD and identifies excessive text-conditioning influence as a root cause of bias. V2's abstract, introduction and conclusion instead foreground the discovery of clustered minority regions and their potential for training-free debiasing. This substantially redefines the central explanatory contribution while retaining the efficiency and image-quality claims.

C2.justification: The mode-test interpretation changes from discovering overlooked low-density noise regions to establishing locally clustered minority regions. V2 adds interpretations of human and simultaneous-debiasing results. It removes v1's explicit limitation that severe training-data bias, exemplified by nurses, reduces effectiveness, retaining only a broader qualification about studying gender and race.

D1.justification: V2 documents model-specific tau values, SD3 encoder handling, pooled conditioning, the SD3 checkpoint and scheduler, and H100 hardware. V1's explicit SD2 masking exception and once-every-three-steps schedule are no longer documented. The baseline code links, checkpoint information and most common settings remain.

R1.justification: V2 adds a bias-analysis subsection distinguishing prior output-bias studies from its exploration of training-free debiasing potential. It adds references covering DALL-Eval, generative-model risks, Gemini and CMMD, and removes the FID reference. The principal debiasing literature and training-based versus training-free positioning remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, analysis narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten around minority regions and weak guidance. The title and author list change, the former experimental Section 5 becomes Section 4.3, and the appendices are reorganized with new evaluation subsections.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the conceptual overview, merges CADS plots and examples, redesigns ablation displays and consolidates qualitative figures. It adds a cross-model summary table, joint-debiasing and human-evaluation tables, and survey screenshots. These substantially change the visual presentation beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: SD3 testing, simultaneous-debiasing experiments and human evaluation broaden the evidence, especially beyond automated demographic classification. However, v2 removes useful cross-model design analyses and the explicit severe-bias limitation, leaves markedly weaker prompt-generalization results unexplained, and introduces a Table 2 average inconsistent with its rows and Table S1. These gains and reporting losses do not support a reliable net quality judgment.
